characters: Mariama: a 12-year-old girl in a school uniform and headscarf, holding a notebook.
Abdul-Rahman: her classmate, 12, in a white shirt and a white cap, with a small sketchbook.
Mr Iddrisu: their teacher, in a long shirt, with a camera he keeps in his bag.
Alhaji Seidu: an elder of Larabanga, about 70, in a white robe and cap, with prayer beads.
Larabanga Mosque: a small whitewashed earth mosque with two pyramid-shaped towers and many buttresses, under a wide blue sky.

culturalNotes: Larabanga Mosque is a real place of worship in the Savannah Region of Ghana. The children, teacher and Alhaji Seidu are invented. Visitors should follow the community’s guidance.

reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?

The story avoids giving 1421 as fact; confirm if any scholarly source offers a different date.

teacherGuide.overview: A heritage mystery with two layers: a date known only through tradition, and a science puzzle about why cement damaged a mud building. It teaches respect and evidence together.
learningGoals: Describe how earthen buildings work and why materials matter.
Explain the difference between a tradition and a documented date.
Describe respectful behaviour at a place of worship.
beforeReading: Ask: why do some old mud buildings last for centuries?
whileReading: At page 6, ask learners to explain why cement and mud do not mix well.
afterReading: Build two mud-brick samples, coat one with cement or plastic, and discuss which dries better (adult supervision).
Interview a community elder about a building they care about, with permission.
discussion: What are different ways to check a date?
How should visitors behave at a mosque?
reflection: What building in your community deserves care?

mathsExtension.task: The mosque measures about 8 m by 8 m. What is its floor area?
If a legend says a building is 600 years old, in what century was it built? (Use 2026.)

support: Provide a labelled diagram of the mosque and its parts.
stretch: Compare earth, cement and stone as building materials, listing pros and cons for a hot, dry climate.

culturalNotes: Larabanga Mosque is a real place of worship in the Savannah Region of Ghana. The children, teacher and Alhaji Seidu are invented. Visitors should follow the community’s guidance.
The story reports the community’s traditions with respect and shows that a date can rest on tradition even when no written record is available.
localiseThis: Visit only with permission and follow local guidance on dress, shoes and photography.
Do not treat the building as a tourist toy; it is a living place of worship.

whatWeKnow: The mosque is built of adobe and timber in the Sudanic style.
A cement coating in the 1970s trapped moisture and the building was damaged; it was restored traditionally.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: The documented date of the first building, since the date we found rests on tradition.

factCheck.claim: Larabanga Mosque is in West Gonja District, Savannah Region; it is Sudanic-style adobe about 8 m by 8 m with two pyramid-shaped towers and twelve buttresses; the founding story concerns the trader Ayuba’s dream; a date of 1421 appears but rests on tradition; a Quran is said by local belief to have been sent in 1650; 1970s cement coating trapped moisture; a storm in September 2002 destroyed the mihrab and minaret; the restoration was led by the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board with CRAterre’s advice and World Monuments Fund support.
factCheck.explanation: From Wikipedia’s article on Larabanga Mosque; the dates 1421 and 1650 are treated as tradition.
factCheck.reference: Wikipedia, “Larabanga Mosque”; confirm with the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board.
